content.narrative_summary: This page summarizes updated recommendations for lipid management, including newer pharmacological approaches and more intensive LDL-C reduction targets. The top table compares previous versus current guideline recommendations for hypertriglyceridaemia treatment, heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia (FH) management (including PCSK9–targeted therapies), dyslipidaemia treatment in older adults, and lipid-lowering therapy post-acute coronary syndrome. Below, new sections are introduced on the use of non-invasive cardiovascular imaging, lipid biology and pathophysiology, novel lipid-modifying medications, and the role of inflammation. section_headings: 4.1.2 How to use the risk estimation charts
content.narrative_summary: The text warns that SCORE overestimates cardiovascular risk in older adults (>65 years) and recommends careful clinical evaluation before treatment in the elderly. The Guidelines include illustrative charts for older people (Figures 1 and 2). HDL-C can improve risk estimation; electronic HeartScore has been modified to include HDL-C as a continuous variable. Extremely high HDL-C (>2.3 mmol/L or 90 mg/dL) appears associated with increased ASCVD risk and thus cannot be used as a risk predictor.

section_headings: 4.2.1 Role of non-invasive cardiovascular imaging techniques in the assessment of total cardiovascular disease risk
content.narrative_summary: Non-invasive imaging techniques such as non-contrast computed tomography can detect coronary artery calcification and assess atherosclerotic burden, improving risk discrimination and reclassification despite no randomized trials demonstrating reduced hard outcomes. Ultrasound assessment of carotid or femoral plaque burden and carotid intima–media thickness also predicts cardiovascular events. In asymptomatic patients at low or moderate risk, imaging may influence statin eligibility decisions from both clinician and patient perspectives, with data showing 41–57% of those with a CAC score of zero would otherwise qualify for statin therapy and event rates over 10 years.

section_headings: 5.3 Evidence for the causal effects of lipids and lipoproteins on the risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease
5.3.1 Low-density lipoprotein cholesterol and risk of atherosclerosis
5.3.2 Triglyceride-rich lipoproteins and risk of atherosclerosis
content.narrative_summary: The narrative explains that retention of ApoB-containing lipoproteins in the arterial wall drives atherosclerotic plaque growth in proportion to circulating concentrations and duration of exposure. Lowering LDL-C reduces ASCVD risk proportionally to absolute LDL-C reduction, supported by biological, experimental, and Mendelian randomization evidence. The clinical benefit of LDL-C–lowering therapies correlates with reduction in LDL particle mass and ApoB. Triglyceride-rich VLDL particles carry most circulating TGs; plasma TG concentration reflects ApoB-containing TG-rich lipoproteins. Elevated TGs are associated with increased ASCVD risk, but this effect is largely mediated by non-HDL-C.

Section 5.3.3 notes that although observational epidemiology shows an inverse association between HDL-C and ASCVD, Mendelian randomization and clinical trials have not proven a causal benefit of raising HDL-C. Section 5.3.4 describes Lp(a) structure, its pro-atherogenic and pro-inflammatory effects, strong genetic inheritance, and evidence that elevated Lp(a) is causally linked to greater ASCVD risk, with emerging trials exploring meaningful reduction. Section 5.4 introduces laboratory measurement of lipids, and 5.4.1 emphasizes direct quantification of ApoB-containing lipoproteins (including VLDL, TG-rich remnants, and LDL) as a practical approach to estimate atherogenic particle number.

section_headings: 5.5 Recommendations for measuring lipids and lipoproteins to estimate risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease
content.narrative_summary: Plasma lipoprotein concentrations are estimated by measuring cholesterol content (TC, HDL-C, TG) and calculating LDL-C using the Friedewald formula, though this has limitations at high TG levels (>4.5 mmol/L or >400 mg/dL), in non-fasting samples, and at low LDL-C; direct enzymatic LDL-C assays and non-HDL-C alternatives can address these issues. Non-fasting sampling produces small TG increases (~0.3 mmol/L) and is generally acceptable for risk screening, but caution is needed for certain analytes and in metabolic syndrome, diabetes, or hypertriglyceridaemia. To estimate ASCVD risk and guide therapy, TC and HDL-C should be measured for SCORE-based algorithms; LDL-C (calculated or direct) should be assessed to identify high-risk individuals and monitor LDL-C–lowering therapy; TG should be measured to detect elevated atherogenic ApoB-containing lipoproteins, recognizing that calculated LDL-C may underestimate risk in high-TG, diabetic, obese, or very low LDL-C states.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for lipid analyses for cardiovascular disease risk estimation

rows.recommendation: TC is to be used for the estimation of total CV risk by means of the SCORE system.
HDL-C analysis is recommended to further refine risk estimation using the online SCORE system.
LDL-C analysis is recommended as the primary lipid analysis method for screening, diagnosis, and management.
TG analysis is recommended as part of the routine lipid analysis process.
Non-HDL-C evaluation is recommended for risk assessment, particularly in people with high TG levels, DM, obesity, or very low LDL-C levels.

ApoB analysis is recommended for risk assessment, particularly in people with high TG levels, DM, obesity, metabolic syndrome, or very low LDL-C levels. It can be used as an alternative to LDL-C, if available, as the primary measurement for screening, diagnosis, and management, and may be preferred over non-HDL-C in people with high TG levels, DM, obesity, or very low LDL-C levels.

Lp(a) measurement should be considered at least once in each adult person’s lifetime to identify those with very high inherited Lp(a) levels >180 mg/dL (>430 nmol/L) who may have a lifetime risk of ASCVD equivalent to the risk associated with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia.
Lp(a) should be considered in selected patients with a family history of premature CVD, and for reclassification in people who are borderline between moderate and high-risk.

section_headings: 7 Lifestyle modifications to improve the plasma lipid profile
content.narrative_summary: The page continues a discussion on tailored lipid management goals based on total cardiovascular (CV) risk. It highlights that lowering LDL-C beyond previous targets is associated with fewer ASCVD events, recommending at least a 50% LDL-C reduction and specific absolute LDL-C goals: <1.4 mmol/L for very-high-risk patients, <1.0 mmol/L for those with a second ASCVD event within 2 years, <1.8 mmol/L for high-risk, <2.6 mmol/L for moderate-risk, and <3.0 mmol/L for low-risk individuals. Secondary targets for non-HDL-C and ApoB are defined (e.g., non-HDL-C <2.2 mmol/L, <2.6 mmol/L, and <3.4 mmol/L for very-high, high, and moderate CV risk; ApoB <65, <80, and <100 mg/dL, respectively). 8.1.4 Adverse effects and interactions of statins
content.narrative_summary: Statins produce pleiotropic anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effects in vitro and in experimental systems, though clinical relevance is unproven. Meta-analyses, including the CTT IPD of >170 000 participants, demonstrate that each 1 mmol/L LDL-C reduction yields ~22% fewer major vascular events and ~10% lower total mortality over 5 years, with proportional benefits across risk groups and a legacy effect. A proposed management scheme includes CV risk assessment, goal setting, patient involvement, regimen choice (including ezetimibe or PCSK9 inhibitors), and dose up-titration. Drug selection should consider patient condition, comorbidities, tolerability, local practice, and cost. Adverse effects relate to absorption, metabolism (CYP450), interactions, and muscle toxicity. Myopathy and rare rhabdomyolysis (CK >10× ULN) occur, with SAMS reported in 10–15% observationally but are unreliable due to study design. Blinded RCTs show minimal risk.

content.narrative_summary: Ezetimibe inhibits intestinal uptake of dietary and biliary cholesterol by interacting with NPC1L1 at the brush border, reducing cholesterol delivery to the liver and upregulating LDL receptor expression, leading to increased LDL clearance. In monotherapy (10 mg/day) it lowers LDL-C by 15–22%, raises HDL-C by ~3%, reduces TGs by ~8%, and lowers total cholesterol by ~13%. Added to statin therapy it provides an extra 21–27% LDL-C reduction and, in outcome trials (SEAS, SHARP, IMPROVE-IT), yields modest reductions in cardiovascular events. Ezetimibe (10 mg/day) is well absorbed, extensively converted to glucuronide, with no significant drug–food, age, sex or race interactions, and minimal liver or renal dose adjustments. Bile acid sequestrants (cholestyramine, colestipol, colesevelam) bind bile acids in the intestine, blocking reabsorption, increasing hepatic cholesterol demand and LDL receptor expression; at typical doses they reduce LDL-C by 18–25%, have little effect on HDL-C, may mildly increase TGs, and colesevelam can lower glucose in hyperglycemic patients. rows.supporting_text:
If ALT < 3× ULN:
• Continue therapy.
• Recheck liver enzymes in 4–6 weeks.
If ALT rises to ≥ 3× ULN:
• Stop lipid-lowering therapy or reduce dose and recheck liver enzymes within 4–6 weeks.
• Cautious reintroduction of therapy may be considered after ALT has returned to normal.
• If ALT remains elevated check for the other reasons.

rows.recommendation: How often should CK be measured in patients taking lipid-lowering drugs?
rows.supporting_text:
Pre-treatment:
• Before starting therapy.
• If baseline CK is > 4× ULN, do not start drug therapy; recheck.
Monitoring:
• Routine monitoring of CK is not necessary.
• Check CK if patient develops myalgia.
Be alert regarding myopathy and CK elevation in patients at risk, such as: elderly patients, those on concomitant interfering therapy, multiple medications, liver or renal disease, or athletes.

rows.recommendation: What if CK becomes elevated in a person taking lipid-lowering drugs?
rows.supporting_text:
Re-evaluate indication for statin treatment.
If ≥ 4× ULN:
• If CK > 10× ULN: stop treatment, check renal function, and monitor CK every 2 weeks.
• If CK < 10× ULN: if no symptoms, continue lipid-lowering therapy while monitoring CK between 2 and 6 weeks.
• If CK < 10× ULN: if symptoms present, stop statin and monitor normalization of CK, before rechallenge with a lower statin dose.
• Consider the possibility of transient CK elevation for other reasons such as exertion.
• Consider myopathy if CK remains elevated.
• Consider combination therapy or an alternative drug.
If < 4× ULN:
• If no muscle symptoms, continue statin (patient should be alerted to report symptoms; check CK).
• If muscle symptoms, monitor symptoms and CK regularly.
• If symptoms persist, stop statin and re-evaluate symptoms after 6 weeks; re-evaluate indication for statin treatment.
• Consider rechallenge with the same or another statin.
• Consider low-dose statin, alternate day or once/twice weekly dosing regimen, or combination therapy.
For details on CK elevation and treatment of muscular symptoms during statin treatment see algorithm in Supplementary Figure 4.

Regular checks of HbA1c or glucose should be considered in patients at high-risk of developing diabetes, and on high-dose statin treatment.

rows.recommendation: Total risk estimation using a risk estimation system such as SCORE is recommended for asymptomatic adults aged >40 years without evidence of CVD, DM, CKD, FH, or LDL >4.9 mmol/L (>190 mg/dL).

High- and very-high-risk individuals may be identified on the basis of documented CVD, DM, moderate-to-severe renal disease, very high levels of individual risk factors, FH, or a high SCORE risk, and are a priority for advice and management of all risk factors.
Risk scores developed for the general population are not recommended for CV risk assessment in patients with DM or FH.
TC is to be used for the estimation of total CV risk by means of the SCORE system.
HDL-C analysis is recommended to further refine risk estimation using the online SCORE system.
LDL-C analysis is recommended as the primary lipid analysis method for screening, diagnosis, and management.
TG analysis is recommended as a part of the routine lipid analysis approach.
Non-HDL-C evaluation is recommended for risk assessment, particularly in people with high TG levels, DM, obesity, or very low LDL-C levels.

ApoB analysis is recommended for risk assessment, particularly in people with high TG levels, DM, obesity, or MetS, or very low LDL-C levels. It can be used as an alternative to LDL-C, if available, as the primary measurement for screening, diagnosis, and management, and may be preferred over non-HDL-C in people with high TG levels, DM, obesity, or very low LDL-C levels.
In secondary prevention for patients at very-high risk, an LDL-C reduction of ≥50% from baseline and an LDL-C goal of <1.4 mmol/L (<55 mg/dL) are recommended.
In primary prevention for individuals at very-high risk, an LDL-C reduction of ≥50% from baseline and an LDL-C goal of <1.4 mmol/L (<55 mg/dL) are recommended.
In patients at high risk, an LDL-C reduction of ≥50% from baseline and an LDL-C goal of <1.8 mmol/L (<70 mg/dL) are recommended.
It is recommended that a high-intensity statin is prescribed up to the highest tolerated dose to reach the goals set for the specific level of risk.
If the goals are not achieved with the maximum tolerated dose of a statin, combination with ezetimibe is recommended.
For secondary prevention in patients at very-high risk not achieving their goal on a maximum tolerated dose of a statin and ezetimibe, a combination with a PCSK9 inhibitor is recommended.

For very-high-risk FH patients (that is, with ASCVD or with another major risk factor) who do not achieve their goal on a maximum tolerated dose of a statin and ezetimibe, a combination with a PCSK9 inhibitor is recommended.
Statin treatment is recommended as the first drug of choice for reducing CVD risk in high-risk individuals with HTG [TGs >2.3 mmol/L (>200 mg/dL)].

It is recommended that a diagnosis of FH is considered in patients with CHD aged <55 years for men and <60 years for women, in people with relatives with premature fatal or non-fatal CVD, in people with relatives having tendon xanthomas, in people with severely elevated LDL-C levels [in adults >5 mmol/L (>190 mg/dL), in children >4 mmol/L (>150 mg/dL)], and in first-degree relatives of FH patients.
It is recommended that FH is diagnosed using clinical criteria and confirmed, when possible, with DNA analysis.
Once the index case is diagnosed, family cascade screening is recommended.
It is recommended that FH patients with ASCVD or who have another major risk factor are treated as very-high-risk, and those with no prior ASCVD or other risk factors as high-risk.

recommendation_tables.title: Lipid-lowering therapy recommendations

rows.recommendation: For FH patients with ASCVD who are at very-high risk, treatment to achieve a ≥50% reduction from baseline and an LDL-C <1.4 mmol/L (<55 mg/dL) is recommended. If goals cannot be achieved, a drug combination is recommended.
Treatment with a PCSK9 inhibitor is recommended in very-high risk FH patients if the treatment goal is not achieved on a maximally tolerated statin plus ezetimibe.
In children, testing for FH is recommended from the age of 5 years, or earlier if HoFH is suspected.
Treatment with statins is recommended for older people with ASCVD in the same way as for younger patients.
Treatment with statins is recommended for primary prevention, according to the level of risk, in older people aged ≤75 years.

It is recommended that the statin is started at a low dose if there is significant renal impairment and/or the potential for drug interactions, and then titrated upwards to achieve LDL-C treatment goals.
In patients with T2DM at very-high risk,c an LDL-C reduction of ≥50% from baseline and an LDL-C goal of <1.4 mmol/L (<55 mg/dL) is recommended.
In patients with T2DM at high risk,c an LDL-C reduction of ≥50% from baseline and an LDL-C goal of <1.8 mmol/L (<70 mg/dL) is recommended.
Statins are recommended in patients with T1DM who are at high or very-high risk.c
Statin therapy is not recommended in pre-menopausal patients with or without DM who are considering pregnancy, or not using adequate contraception.

In all ACS patients without any contraindication or definite history of intolerance, it is recommended that high-dose statin therapy is initiated or continued as early as possible, regardless of initial LDL-C values.
If the LDL-C goal is not achieved after 4–6 weeks with the maximally tolerated statin dose, combination with ezetimibe is recommended.
If the LDL-C goal is not achieved after 4–6 weeks despite maximal tolerated statin therapy and ezetimibe, adding a PCSK9 inhibitor is recommended.
Patients with a history of ischaemic stroke or TIA are at very-high risk of ASCVD, particularly recurrent ischaemic stroke, so it is recommended that they receive intensive LDL-C-lowering therapy.
Initiation of lipid-lowering therapy is not recommended in patients with HF in the absence of other indications for their use.

Initiation of lipid-lowering treatment is not recommended in patients with aortic valvular stenosis without CAD to slow progression of aortic valve stenosis in the absence of other indications for their use.
It is recommended that patients with stage 3–5 CKD are considered to be at high or very-high risk of ASCVD.
The use of statins or statin/ezetimibe combination is recommended in patients with non-dialysis-dependent stage 3–5 CKD.
In patients with dialysis-dependent CKD who are free of ASCVD, commencement of statin therapy is not recommended.

In patients with PAD, lipid-lowering therapy—including a maximum tolerated dose of a statin, plus ezetimibe, or a combination with a PCSK9 inhibitor if needed—is recommended to reduce the risk of ASCVD events.
The use of lipid-lowering drugs only on the basis of the presence of CIID is not recommended.
It is recommended that SMIs are used as modifiers for estimating total ASCVD risk.
It is recommended that the same guidelines for the management of total ASCVD risk are used in patients with SMI as are used in patients without such disease.
It is recommended that in patients with SMI, intensified attention is paid to adherence to lifestyle changes and to compliance with drug treatment.
